The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Flexport Leadership Turmoil

Dave Clark, the former Amazon executive who was ousted as CEO of Flexport just a year into the job, fired back at the company's founder and board, calling recent reporting on the logistics company "deeply concerning."

Clark made the comments on Monday of the week covered by TechCrunch's October 7, 2023 Week in Review, in a lengthy post on the social media site X. The post followed a CNBC report that had provided new information about his last days at Flexport. Flexport is described as a freight forwarding and customs brokerage startup valued at $8 billion.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. # Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."



---


# Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. The Age's writer called this a compelling point, familiar to anyone who has dodged Microsoft's pleading while setting Chrome and Google as defaults on a new PC, but countered that all of these arguments ignore that Google and its competitors are not on an even playing field: the question remains why users prefer Google, and if the answer is that Google is simply better, the further question is whether that is down to its scale, longevity, ubiquity and all the user data it sucks up, which no other company could possibly match.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. # US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.

"They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."



---


# Platform Owners Should Treat Developers As Partners

Tim Sweeney argued that any tech company, Apple and Google included, would be much better off in the long term if it viewed developers as awesome partners and did everything it could to support and empower them rather than get in their way financially — and said the opposite behavior at Apple and Google is what has disappointed him most.

His grounds are a comparison and a diagnosis. The comparison is Microsoft: even at the peak of the antitrust trial against Microsoft, he said, Microsoft was awesome to developers — always respectful, giving developers a great deal and treating them as partners — so that even as Microsoft was crushing corporate competitors, the developer experience was excellent. The Verge appended an editor's note that Netscape might feel differently. The diagnosis is that Google and Apple both treat developers as adversaries, trying to attack developer revenue streams and prevent them from competing with the platforms' own products, and have built massive self-preferencing schemes around excluding developers and disadvantaging third parties — which Sweeney calls very shortsighted. The warrant is that a platform's own long-term position improves when its developers thrive, and Sweeney offers Epic's own conduct as the demonstration: this has been Epic's philosophy with Unreal Engine and the Epic Games Store, where Epic wants to be "a cool partner that helps other companies succeed the way we do." The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. When Musk invested in DeepMind he broke his own informal rule that he would not invest in any company he didn't run himself, and the downsides were already apparent when, only a month or so after his birthday spat with Larry Page, he again found himself face to face with his former friend. The occasion was the first meeting of DeepMind's ethics board on 14 August 2015, a board set up at the insistence of the startup's founders to ensure their technology did no harm after the sale. The members convened in a conference room just outside Musk's office at SpaceX, but that is where Musk's control ended: when Google bought DeepMind it bought the whole thing, and Musk was out, financially ahead but unhappy. Three Google executives now firmly in control of DeepMind were there, Page, Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder and Tesla investor, and Eric Schmidt, Google's chair, along with other attendees including Reid Hoffman, another PayPal founder, and Toby Ord, an Australian philosopher studying "existential risk".

The DeepMind founders reported that they were pushing ahead with their work but were aware the technology carried serious risks. Mustafa Suleyman gave a presentation called "The Pitchforkers Are Coming", telling the board that AI could lead to an explosion in disinformation and fretting that as the technology replaced countless jobs in coming years the public would accuse Google of stealing their livelihoods, so Google would need to share its wealth with the millions who could no longer find work and provide a "universal basic income". Musk agreed, but it was pretty clear the Google guests were not prepared to embark on a redistribution of their wealth: Schmidt said he thought the worries were completely overblown, and Page, in his usual whisper, agreed, arguing AI would create more jobs than it took away. Eight months later DeepMind had a breakthrough that stunned the AI community and the world, when a DeepMind machine called AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the ancient game of Go, a match streamed over the internet and watched by 200 million people across the globe, though most researchers had assumed AI needed another 10 years to muster the ingenuity to do that; the South Korean professional Lee Se-dol played Go against AlphaGo in March 2016.

# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

Tim Sweeney argued that any tech company, Apple and Google included, would be much better off in the long term if it viewed developers as awesome partners and did everything it could to support and empower them rather than get in their way financially — and said the opposite behavior at Apple and Google is what has disappointed him most.

Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. # Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.

# Bankman-Fried's Conduct On Direct Examination

On October 28th, 2023, before the cross-examination had even begun, Judge Lewis Kaplan had already instructed Sam Bankman-Fried to answer the question he was being asked by his own lawyer — which The Verge's reporter called honestly kind of incredible, a man torpedoing his own credibility on direct testimony. The count of "Objection, narrative!" to Bankman-Fried's answers, followed by "Sustained," stood at three; the main thing clear so far, she wrote, was that he really loves the sound of his own voice, and that sometimes when he says "we," he only means himself.

The scolding was a pattern across two days. The day before, during an evidentiary hearing, Bankman-Fried had been repeatedly scolded by Kaplan for not answering prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's questions on cross-examination; on this day he was scolded for not answering his own counsel Mark Cohen's questions on direct, and he occasionally interrupted Cohen with "yes" and "yup." Much of the morning went on vocabulary — explaining "Amazon Web Services" and "database" was a bit too detail-oriented — and when Bankman-Fried tried to define "market manipulation," Kaplan told the jury that he, the judge, was the final authority on that.

In fairness, the reporter added, he was clearer and much easier to understand than at the evidentiary hearing the day before, with a minimum of word salad; she could not tell whether he was more relaxed or simply more rehearsed, and said she would be watching to see whether he became much less coherent once Sassoon got him on cross. The jury watched all of it intently.

# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."

# Can Sun's Testimony On Fabricated Justifications

Former FTX lawyer Can Sun testified that during the days in November when the exchange imploded, Bankman-Fried — then trying to raise money from the private equity group Apollo, which wanted an explanation for what had happened — came to him and asked him to come up with justifications for the missing funds. That request, Sun said, "basically confirmed my suspicions that had been rising all day" that Bankman-Fried had purloined the funds.

Sun ran Bankman-Fried through possible explanations, including a margin loan program, and explained that none of them could fit the actual situation — for instance, Alameda had borrowed more from FTX than had ever been in the margin loan program. He said Bankman-Fried acknowledged their conversation with a "yup, yup": "I was expecting a bigger response, but it was very muted." After that, Sun testified, Singh spilled the beans that Alameda had withdrawn assets that included the customer funds. Sun quit the next day, and, like Yedidia, testified with immunity.

The jury then saw the fabrication deployed in public: a Good Morning America appearance by Bankman-Fried on December 1st, 2022, in which he tried to justify the missing funds through the margin loan program. The Verge's reporter called it such a flimsy excuse that even George Stephanopoulos could see through it, and described Sun's testimony as brief and explosive.

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. # ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. CNET found itself in controversy after Futurism reported the publication was publishing articles under a mysterious byline completely generated by AI, and Red Ventures, the private equity company that owns CNET, was accused of using ChatGPT for SEO farming even where the information was incorrect. # Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. # OpenAI's Founding And Its 2023 Board Crisis

The Rosewood hotel dinner led to the creation of a startup called OpenAI later that year; backed by hundreds of millions of dollars from Elon Musk and other funders, the lab promised to protect the world from Larry Page's vision. Thanks to its ChatGPT chatbot, OpenAI has fundamentally changed the technology industry and introduced the world to the risks and potential of artificial intelligence, and it is valued at more than $US80 billion, about $A123 billion, according to two people familiar with the company's latest funding round. Musk and Sam Altman's partnership did not survive, and the two have since stopped speaking. Altman's own gloss on such splits: "There is disagreement, mistrust, egos. The closer people are to being pointed in the same direction, the more contentious the disagreements are. You see this in sects and religious orders. # GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. # Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

# DeepMind's Ethics Board And Its Single Meeting In 2015

When Musk invested in DeepMind he broke his own informal rule that he would not invest in any company he didn't run himself, and the downsides were already apparent when, only a month or so after his birthday spat with Larry Page, he again found himself face to face with his former friend. The occasion was the first meeting of DeepMind's ethics board on 14 August 2015, a board set up at the insistence of the startup's founders to ensure their technology did no harm after the sale. The members convened in a conference room just outside Musk's office at SpaceX, but that is where Musk's control ended: when Google bought DeepMind it bought the whole thing, and Musk was out, financially ahead but unhappy. Three Google executives now firmly in control of DeepMind were there, Page, Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder and Tesla investor, and Eric Schmidt, Google's chair, along with other attendees including Reid Hoffman, another PayPal founder, and Toby Ord, an Australian philosopher studying "existential risk".

The DeepMind founders reported that they were pushing ahead with their work but were aware the technology carried serious risks. Mustafa Suleyman gave a presentation called "The Pitchforkers Are Coming", telling the board that AI could lead to an explosion in disinformation and fretting that as the technology replaced countless jobs in coming years the public would accuse Google of stealing their livelihoods, so Google would need to share its wealth with the millions who could no longer find work and provide a "universal basic income". Musk agreed, but it was pretty clear the Google guests were not prepared to embark on a redistribution of their wealth: Schmidt said he thought the worries were completely overblown, and Page, in his usual whisper, agreed, arguing AI would create more jobs than it took away. Eight months later DeepMind had a breakthrough that stunned the AI community and the world, when a DeepMind machine called AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the ancient game of Go, a match streamed over the internet and watched by 200 million people across the globe, though most researchers had assumed AI needed another 10 years to muster the ingenuity to do that; the South Korean professional Lee Se-dol played Go against AlphaGo in March 2016.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Search As Private Infrastructure, Not A Public Library

The claim is that routing nearly all online information through a single private company has left us arguably worse off than before, because information that is controlled by a private business will always be subject to that business's bottom line — which is exactly why most countries around the world have libraries that are public institutions.

The grounds are a comparison with what the internet was supposed to be. In the beginning it was seen as an improvement on the spirit of the public library: an opportunity to transcend the gatekeepers controlling who could publish a book, allowing mankind to fully connect and share knowledge. Instead, nearly all online information runs through a single company, which assumes a veneer of civic utility, of impassive authority, when it is very much not a neutral entity.

Matt Cutts supplies the insider warrant that the veneer is doing work. "There were so many true believers at Google in the early days," he said. "As companies get big, it gets harder to get things done. Inevitably, people start to think about profit or quarterly numbers." He claimed that, at least while he was there, search quality always came before financial goals, but he believes the public underestimates how Google is shaping what they see: "I deeply, deeply, deeply believe search engines are newspaper-like entities, making editorial decisions." He speculated that the company did not want the public to think too hard about how search works because that awareness "encourages regulators and makes people realize, 'Oh, there's a lot of money here.'"

The consequence is epistemic rather than commercial. There has always been advertising and polemics from cranks, scammers, and liars, but now we see this stuff surfacing alongside truth and we cannot tell the difference, so we move through our lives with a greater sense of distrust and fear and insecurity. At the end of the day, it is Google's world, and the SEOs are only living in it.



---


# Platform Owners Should Treat Developers As Partners

Tim Sweeney argued that any tech company, Apple and Google included, would be much better off in the long term if it viewed developers as awesome partners and did everything it could to support and empower them rather than get in their way financially — and said the opposite behavior at Apple and Google is what has disappointed him most.

His grounds are a comparison and a diagnosis. The comparison is Microsoft: even at the peak of the antitrust trial against Microsoft, he said, Microsoft was awesome to developers — always respectful, giving developers a great deal and treating them as partners — so that even as Microsoft was crushing corporate competitors, the developer experience was excellent. The diagnosis is that Google and Apple both treat developers as adversaries, trying to attack developer revenue streams and prevent them from competing with the platforms' own products, and have built massive self-preferencing schemes around excluding developers and disadvantaging third parties — which Sweeney calls very shortsighted. The warrant is that a platform's own long-term position improves when its developers thrive, and Sweeney offers Epic's own conduct as the demonstration: this has been Epic's philosophy with Unreal Engine and the Epic Games Store, where Epic wants to be "a cool partner that helps other companies succeed the way we do." # Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

Asked what surprised him in the courtroom, Tim Sweeney said the trial confirmed practices he had suspected since around 2018 — when some people called him a conspiracy theorist for saying so — including that Google leaked Epic's conversations to reporters to get negative stories written, paid other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores, and went around paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores.

# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."



---


# Prediction: OpenAI Becomes A Product Company

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. TechCrunch expects the "app store for AI" to be pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models, on the reasoning that OpenAI has an excellent model to work from in Apple's and will follow it all the way to the bank.

More broadly, the prediction is that the caution and academic reserve the previous board exerted will give way to an unseemly lust for markets and customers. Other major companies with AI efforts are expected to follow the same trend — for instance, Gemini/Bard horning in on a ton of Google products — but the writer suspects it will be more pronounced at OpenAI.



---


# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.
