# Bankman-Fried's Conduct On Direct Examination

On October 28th, 2023, before the cross-examination had even begun, Judge Lewis Kaplan had already instructed Sam Bankman-Fried to answer the question he was being asked by his own lawyer — which The Verge's reporter called honestly kind of incredible, a man torpedoing his own credibility on direct testimony. The count of "Objection, narrative!" to Bankman-Fried's answers, followed by "Sustained," stood at three; the main thing clear so far, she wrote, was that he really loves the sound of his own voice, and that sometimes when he says "we," he only means himself.

The scolding was a pattern across two days. The day before, during an evidentiary hearing, Bankman-Fried had been repeatedly scolded by Kaplan for not answering prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's questions on cross-examination; on this day he was scolded for not answering his own counsel Mark Cohen's questions on direct, and he occasionally interrupted Cohen with "yes" and "yup." Much of the morning went on vocabulary — explaining "Amazon Web Services" and "database" was a bit too detail-oriented — and when Bankman-Fried tried to define "market manipulation," Kaplan told the jury that he, the judge, was the final authority on that.

In fairness, the reporter added, he was clearer and much easier to understand than at the evidentiary hearing the day before, with a minimum of word salad; she could not tell whether he was more relaxed or simply more rehearsed, and said she would be watching to see whether he became much less coherent once Sassoon got him on cross. # Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. qid: Which company, reported by TechCrunch, is involved in an antitrust battle where it provided court evidence against claims of hiding discovery items, spent billions to maintain its default search engine status, and is accused of harming news publishers’ revenue through anticompetitive practices?
context:

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

Microsoft, back in the early days of the internet.

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. ---

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.

qid: Who is the individual under 30 who became the richest in the world, reportedly with the intention of using their wealth for the preservation of humanity, but is now facing allegations of fraud and deceit regarding the operations of a crypto exchange, as reported by Fortune, The Verge, and TechCrunch?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.

qid: Who is the individual associated with the cryptocurrency industry who, before the collapse of FTX, portrayed himself as a reliable figure, planned to establish a board with experts for the company without investor directors, was accused of using customer funds to buy out a competitor, and is alleged by the prosecution to have committed fraud for personal gain, with these events being reported by The Verge, CNBC, and TechCrunch?
context:
# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# VC And Lender Testimony As Collateral Risk For Crypto

The Verge argued that calling lenders, venture capitalists and customers to testify — necessary to establish the basis for some charges — might create collateral damage for the crypto industry beyond Bankman-Fried himself.

The grounds are the shape of the indictment and who it drags in: prosecutors allege that Bankman-Fried lied to FTX investors, so some of those investors may be called on to testify, which is not the kind of thing VC big shots generally enjoy. The worked example is Sequoia Capital: if Sequoia did due diligence around its investment in FTX, whatever Bankman-Fried told its partners could be important — was FTX already sending Alameda customer funds at that point, did Bankman-Fried know, and did he tell the VCs at the time? If he told them it wasn't happening, that would establish intent. Hermine Wong, the former head of policy at Coinbase and a former SEC regulator, adds that Binance was also an early investor in FTX and that former executives may be called on to testify as well.



---


# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

# The Timing Trade-Off In Rookie Of The Year Futures Betting

There is a fixed trade-off in when to bet NBA Rookie of the Year futures: the earlier you bet, the better the odds, but you bet without much information that could be key to an educated decision; conversely, if you wait for the data you need for an informed bet, the odds tighten and you see less of a return.

The mechanism is symmetric between bettor and book. When the lines are first released, the season has not started, so there are no statistics, trends or player news — the pre-season odds are so favorable precisely because even the oddsmakers lack the data to craft more specific lines. Once the season starts and you can see how the rookies are performing, you can gather the relevant data; but sportsbooks are gathering the same information and tighten the Rookie of the Year lines in response. So while you can better guess who will hoist the Wilt Chamberlain Trophy, the odds are tighter and your potential return reduced.

Stated as pros and cons: betting early gives an opportunity to find better value and betting odds that are fresh and unadjusted, but carries much higher risk because a player's performance, health and team dynamic can change through the season, and offers limited information. Waiting gives a lot more information for an informed bet and avoids betting on a player not remotely in contention, but reduces the opportunity to find value and the odds may not be as favorable. The range over which this holds is bounded by the individual: it is always important to take your risk tolerance into consideration while weighing the potential rewards, and no matter when you decide to wager, always gather as much information as possible before risking your money.



---


# How Sportsbooks Set And Move Betting Lines

The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds, while other sports betting apps simply copy those lines. The oddsmakers and services use computer models and algorithms that consider analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, matchup data and more to develop the lines and odds. Those lines are then subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that emerges before the game, and a book will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side.

The governing objective is balance rather than prediction. Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet, because that lets the book earn the small profit built into the odds and lines without worrying about which side wins. Sportsbooks want even betting so much that they will move a line or change the odds specifically to draw more bets to the other side.

The relation that matters to a bettor is that books do not all move together. The betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook: one book may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of the money it has taken while another is not, and the lines and odds may even differ right from the jump. That divergence is what creates the chance to book a bet at improved odds or a more favorable line.

The range over which this holds is narrow and specific. When a line moves for a legitimate reason such as an injury or roster move, every sportsbook jumps on board, and it is difficult to find value; when a line moves because of betting patterns, only the sportsbook that saw that betting makes the change, and that is the opportunity. Line shopping is the tool for spotting the second kind: choose a side, shop around at online sportsbooks, compare the lines and odds, and pounce when you find one offering something different and more favorable to your viewpoint.



---


# Why Bettors Should Consider NFL Award Longshots — And Bet Them Small

Sporting News argued on Dec. 5, 2023 that with five weeks left in the regular season there was plenty of time for an NFL award longshot to become a contender, so bettors should consider them — but should keep those bets small.

The grounds for taking longshots seriously are that they are easy to overlook because each award has a favorite or favorites: a longshot may be playing well, but other players have commanded the spotlight, making it easier for them to go unnoticed, and whatever the reason, they have not gotten the credit they deserve. The timing argument follows: if you wait too long before placing a bet, your payout will be a lot less than if you were to roll the dice on a longshot right now.

The counterweight, and the warrant for the sizing advice, is that there is always a reason why a player or several players have relatively short odds — they have been the best at their position throughout the season — and consequently there is just as good a reason why longshots have odds as long as they do. So the recommendation is to keep your bets small, or use a bonus bet if one is available, on longshots; if they do go on to win, you can smile all the way to the bank while telling everyone, "I told you so."

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."

Investors are betting that consumer trading of equity and crypto is rebounding, and are consequently pushing the value of some former startups higher, TechCrunch's Alex wrote in the 9 December 2023 roundup.

# Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

The jury is also sealed off from coverage: Judge Donato explicitly told jurors they are in a "news-free bubble" through mid-December.

# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. # Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. Duane Forrester was at Microsoft from 2007 until 2015, where he helped launch and manage Bing, the perpetual underdog to Google's domination of online search; because he worked as an SEO both before and after his time at Microsoft, he sees the industry from both sides — like an aerospace engineer who spent a few years at the Department of Defense, left for the private sector, and now is much better at winning military contracts. He was the first stop because Google was slow to allow anyone to talk to the writer, possibly because of the giant PR clusterfuck that has been the company's past year: accused by the federal government of being a monopoly, increasingly despised by the public, losing ground to Reddit, TikTok, and large language models.

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.

# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# Prediction: OpenAI Becomes A Product Company

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. TechCrunch expects the "app store for AI" to be pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models, on the reasoning that OpenAI has an excellent model to work from in Apple's and will follow it all the way to the bank.

More broadly, the prediction is that the caution and academic reserve the previous board exerted will give way to an unseemly lust for markets and customers. Other major companies with AI efforts are expected to follow the same trend — for instance, Gemini/Bard horning in on a ton of Google products — but the writer suspects it will be more pronounced at OpenAI.

# Google's Secret OEM And Carrier Deals And Its Deleted Chats

Asked what surprised him in the courtroom, Tim Sweeney said the trial confirmed practices he had suspected since around 2018 — when some people called him a conspiracy theorist for saying so — including that Google leaked Epic's conversations to reporters to get negative stories written, paid other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores, and went around paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores.

Sweeney gave a concrete instance from Epic's own experience: when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with other smartphone manufacturers such as OnePlus and with carriers of all sorts, those partners told Epic they couldn't do a deal because Google had done a secret deal with them. He called it disconcerting to see the extent of bad-faith efforts inside a company of Google's size, saying you would expect a trillion-dollar company to have developed respectable processes and leadership structures providing checks and balances against wrongdoing. Instead, he said, Google employees were "rampantly destroying all their chats on these topics": long conversation threads would start to get into a spicy antitrust issue, somebody would point out that history was on, and the chat would go silent — history turned off so the documents would be destroyed. Sweeney said it was great to see all of that called out in detail at trial.

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. Asked to summarise topical news in early December 2023, Gemini Pro often would not do it, despite having Google Search and Google News at its disposal. It seemed loath to comment on potentially controversial news topics, instead telling users to Google it themselves.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# Where FTX Customer Money Went

Expert witness Peter Easton, a Notre Dame accounting professor who had also assisted in investigating Enron and WorldCom, traced the funds behind the $11.3 billion liability that Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried had known about in June 2022, and presented the breakdown to the jury as a pie chart (the prosecution's exhibit 1045). An earlier and separate use of customer money came in the summer of 2021, when Bankman-Fried bought back FTX shares from Binance, an early investor. Ellison testified that he told her it was "really important," otherwise "Binance would do things to mess with FTX"; she told him Alameda did not have the money, so Bankman-Fried took $1 billion of FTX customer funds to buy Binance out. It was the first time Ellison recalled an amount that large, and she said it was Bankman-Fried's decision, as he was CEO of FTX.

# Adam Yedidia's Testimony And The $8 Billion Bug

Adam Yedidia, the prosecution's second witness, testified that in June 2022 he submitted a report to Bankman-Fried on Signal showing that $8 billion in customer money held in an internal database tracking cash wired to an Alameda account called "fiat at ftx.com" was missing.

Yedidia met Bankman-Fried in college at MIT and the pair remained close friends; assuming a robotic posture on the stand, he said he worked out of FTX's Hong Kong office from January to October of 2021 and then in the Bahamas until the collapse. He referred to a group Signal thread called "People of the House," referring to Bankman-Fried's $35 million penthouse where many employees lived; on who was paying the rent, Yedidia recalled Bankman-Fried saying he "assumed it's just Alameda paying for it in the end." Yedidia said Bankman-Fried had told him, before he began working in the Bahamas in 2019, that he and Ellison had had sex, and asked whether it was a good idea for them to date — Yedidia said no, and Bankman-Fried responded that he was expecting that answer. One of Yedidia's responsibilities was fixing the bug in the code that gave Alameda preferential treatment. He said he and Bankman-Fried spoke about the missing $8 billion at the pickleball court at the resort in Nassau, Bahamas, where he asked his boss if things were OK because it "seemed like a lot of money" from FTX customers was at risk. "Sam said, we were bulletproof last year. We aren't bulletproof this year," Yedidia testified; asked when they would be bulletproof again, Bankman-Fried said he was not sure, but it might be six months to three years. Yedidia said Bankman-Fried appeared "worried or nervous," which was atypical, but that he still trusted Bankman-Fried and Ellison to "handle the situation." On cross-examination, Christian Everdell, Bankman-Fried's attorney, focused on how Yedidia was the one responsible for developing and reviewing the code.

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.

# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."

# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.

Gary Wang told the court that Alameda received advantages through code baked into FTX's software granting it special access to the exchange — "We gave special privileges on FTX that gave unlimited withdrawals on the platform to Alameda" — privileges that ultimately resulted in Alameda owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits.

The structure had several linked parts. Alameda was allowed to withdraw and transfer funds and had a $65 billion line of credit. "When customers deposited USD, it went to Alameda," Wang said. "It existed in the computer code. Alameda could have negative balances and unlimited withdrawals." That "bug" in the code was written by Nishad Singh, FTX's director of engineering, and reviewed by Wang, with Bankman-Fried calling the shots. Wang also told the court about a $1 million personal loan he received and a $200 million to $300 million loan in his name from Alameda that was never deposited into his account but was used to make investments into other companies on behalf of FTX — all done by Bankman-Fried, he testified. The escalation was visible over time: in early 2020 Wang discovered for the first time that Alameda's negative balance exceeded FTX's revenue, an indication that Alameda was taking customer funds, and he brought this to Bankman-Fried's attention several times; in late 2021 he discovered Alameda had withdrawn $3 billion from its $65 billion line of credit. The ownership and authority around it: Wang owned 10% of Alameda while his boss owned the other 90%, his compensation was a base salary of $200,000 per year plus stock, and he owned roughly 17% of FTX — and even though they were co-founders, "ultimately it was Sam's decision to make" when there were disagreements. Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

# Alameda Research's Origins And Naming

Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried said he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time but wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway, and that he is "somewhat introverted, naturally."

The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. I didn't want to call it Sam's Crypto Trading Firm or anything like that. We — there are a lot of competitors and people who we didn't particularly want to know what we were building out because they would race to do it. 'Research' was a sort of generic word, which filled out the company name. And that was — it was far better than the internal name that we had at that point, which was Wireless Mouse." The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. Though Bankman-Fried was CEO and also majority owner, he wanted to be clear that he did not supervise Wang's direct work. After a run of wildly successful arbitrage — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns, per his testimony — he decided to found a cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, figuring he would fail and putting the chance of success at 20 percent, without defining the time period he had in mind.

# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.



---


# David Pakman's Venture Background At CoinFund

On TechCrunch's Chain Reaction podcast, Jacquelyn interviewed David Pakman, managing partner and head of venture investments at CoinFund.

Before CoinFund, Pakman spent 14 years at the venture capital firm Venrock. He also led the Series A and B rounds at Dollar Shave Club, which was acquired by Unilever for $1 billion. And in 1991 he co-created Apple Music when he was part of Apple's system software product marketing group.

# Alameda's Special Privileges Written Into FTX's Code

Gary Wang told the court that Alameda received advantages through code baked into FTX's software granting it special access to the exchange — "We gave special privileges on FTX that gave unlimited withdrawals on the platform to Alameda" — privileges that ultimately resulted in Alameda owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits.

The structure had several linked parts. Alameda was allowed to withdraw and transfer funds and had a $65 billion line of credit. "When customers deposited USD, it went to Alameda," Wang said. "It existed in the computer code. Alameda could have negative balances and unlimited withdrawals." That "bug" in the code was written by Nishad Singh, FTX's director of engineering, and reviewed by Wang, with Bankman-Fried calling the shots. Wang also told the court about a $1 million personal loan he received and a $200 million to $300 million loan in his name from Alameda that was never deposited into his account but was used to make investments into other companies on behalf of FTX — all done by Bankman-Fried, he testified. In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.
