# Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.
- **Concrete availability signals** — corpus reporting marks a launch's completion with specific, checkable facts: a price, an order date, or a shipping date, e.g. the Steam Deck OLED being "available to order on November 16th" with shipping "as orders start to roll in," or the Echo Pop Kids being "available for purchase, starting at $49.99."

# Danny Sullivan, From Journalist To Google Liaison

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

# Google's Denial That Ad Keyword Matching Affects Organic Results

Google's official search liaison Danny Sullivan rebutted the allegation that Google manipulates search to maximise ad revenue by denying the causal link it depends on: in a post on X, he said ad systems do not affect the organic results — the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored.

"Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads," Sullivan said. "A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query." He also defended query interpretation on its own terms: "It's no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning… If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that's not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren't even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help." The Age noted the claim being answered comes from Megan Gray, herself a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google; she admits she may have misinterpreted the evidence but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. The paper granted that some search queries result in more ads than others and that which ads you get can vary wildly by request — the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads — but noted Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. # iPhone Setup And The Absence Of A Search Engine Choice Screen

Eddy Cue acknowledged on the stand that the ISA didn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup — and said he wouldn't want to do that anyway, because "we try to get people up and running as fast as possible" and "setup is just critical stuff."

Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw built to that answer through a series of questions about the iPhone setup process, using three screenshots: the Appearance screen that appears when you first boot up an iPhone so you can pick font sizes, the location-tracking prompt that appears when you open Maps, and the App Tracking Transparency pop-up that tells you when an app wants to collect your data. Cue objected to all of these being considered part of setup, but Bellshaw's point was that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, and that search could be one of them. Cue argued that showing people a bunch of search engines they had never heard of would just be a bad user experience — even he couldn't remember the names of some of the alternatives to Google — and said, "We make Google be the default search engine because we've always thought it was the best. We pick the best one and let users easily change it." The Verge noted that "easily" is a persistent point of contention in the trial: DuckDuckGo's CEO, who testified the week before, claimed it takes "too many steps" to switch.

# NBA Props And Futures: What They Cover And When To Bet Them

NBA player and team props are growing in popularity, and sportsbooks are providing more NBA props than ever, because it is much easier to focus on a single player and how he will perform than on the entire team. Player props might cover how many points a player scores or how many rebounds he pulls down, typically provided in an over/under format. Team props range from which team will score the first bucket to the total points scored in a quarter to which team will lead at halftime, with the selection often robust, especially when high-profile teams play.

Futures bets are bets on events that will happen in the future, and Rookie of the Year is only one of them: legal online sportsbooks carry a wide selection of NBA futures. They can usually be bet throughout the year, including well before the season starts and through the regular season, and the further away from the event, the more likely you are to find heavier odds in your favor.

Alongside futures, bettors can wager on many NBA markets during the regular season and postseason. Game lines — moneylines, point spreads and totals — are the most popular, but team and player props, parlays and more are also available. The NBA is the second-most popular odds market to bet on in the US, behind NFL betting odds, which means every online betting site always has a great selection of NBA odds.

# DeepMind's Founding And Thiel's Investment

In 2010 Demis Hassabis and two colleagues, all living in Britain, were looking for money to start building "artificial general intelligence", a machine that could do anything the brain could do, at a time when few people were interested in AI because after a half-century of research the field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain. Some scientists and thinkers had nonetheless become fixated on AI's downsides, and many, including the three young men, had a connection to Eliezer Yudkowsky, an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher who led a community calling themselves Rationalists or, later, effective altruists; they believed AI could find a cure for cancer or solve climate change but worried that AI bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Peter Thiel, enormously wealthy through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Musk in the early days of PayPal, had developed a fascination with the singularity, the science-fiction trope describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity, and with his funding Yudkowsky had expanded his AI lab and created an annual conference on the singularity; one of Hassabis' colleagues had met Yudkowsky years before and snagged them speaking spots at that conference, ensuring an invitation to Thiel's party, where Yudkowsky introduced Hassabis to Thiel. Assuming many guests would be trying to squeeze their host for money, Hassabis' strategy was to arrange another meeting: he told Thiel there was a deep tension between the bishop and the knight, pieces carrying the same value whose strengths the best players understood to be vastly different. Charmed, Thiel invited the group back the next day, gathering in the kitchen where their host, just finished with his morning workout and still sweating in a shiny tracksuit, was handed a Diet Coke by a butler; the three made their pitch and soon Thiel and his venture capital firm agreed to put £1.4 million, about $A2.7 million, into their startup, making him their first major investor.

They named the company DeepMind, a nod to "deep learning", a way for AI systems to learn skills by analysing large amounts of data, to neuroscience, and to the Deep Thought supercomputer from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, and by the spring of 2010 they were building their dream machine, wholeheartedly believing that because they understood the risks they were uniquely positioned to protect the world. Mustafa Suleyman, one of the three founders, said "I don't see this as a contradictory position. There are huge benefits to come from these technologies. The goal is not to eliminate them or pause their development. The goal is to mitigate the downsides." Having won over Thiel, Hassabis worked his way into Musk's orbit: about two years later they met at a conference organised by Thiel's investment fund, which had also put money into SpaceX, and Hassabis secured a tour of SpaceX headquarters, after which, with rocket hulls hanging from the ceiling, the two lunched in the cafeteria; Musk explained his plan to colonise Mars to escape overpopulation and other dangers on Earth, and Hassabis replied that the plan would work so long as superintelligent machines didn't follow and destroy humanity on Mars too. Musk was speechless, not having thought about that particular danger, and soon invested in DeepMind alongside Thiel so he could be closer to the creation of the technology.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Alameda Research's Origins And Naming

Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried said he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time but wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway, and that he is "somewhat introverted, naturally."

The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. I didn't want to call it Sam's Crypto Trading Firm or anything like that. We — there are a lot of competitors and people who we didn't particularly want to know what we were building out because they would race to do it. 'Research' was a sort of generic word, which filled out the company name. And that was — it was far better than the internal name that we had at that point, which was Wireless Mouse." The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. Though Bankman-Fried was CEO and also majority owner, he wanted to be clear that he did not supervise Wang's direct work. After a run of wildly successful arbitrage — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns, per his testimony — he decided to found a cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, figuring he would fail and putting the chance of success at 20 percent, without defining the time period he had in mind.

# The 2016 ISA Renegotiation And Its Revenue-Share Dispute

Eddy Cue testified that when Apple and Google renegotiated the ISA, Apple wanted a higher percentage of the revenue Google made from the Apple users it directed to the search engine, while Sundar Pichai wanted to keep the deal as it was; the two eventually compromised on some other number that was not disclosed in open court, and Google has been paying Apple that amount since.

Discussion of specific numbers was reserved for closed court sessions. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw asked Cue whether he would have walked away from the deal if the two sides couldn't agree on a revenue-share figure, and Cue said he had never really considered that an option: "I always felt like it was in Google's best interest, and our best interest, to get a deal done." Cue also argued that the deal was about more than economics, that Apple never seriously considered switching to another provider or building its own search product, and that "certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" — adding that there still isn't one.

# Film Awards Season

## Definition

Film awards season is the recurring stretch of the film-industry calendar in which press coverage frames new releases as Oscar or Academy Award contenders — flagging some as deliberately positioned to win ("Oscar bait") and speculating on which will actually take home a prize — while a person's past Academy Award wins and nominations continue to be cited as a lasting professional credential.

## Context

In the corpus the season shows up mainly as a lens critics apply to late-2023 releases: Polygon calls Poor Things "the unlikeliest but most effective Oscar bait" and says it is "tipped to win a few real Oscars," and in a separate piece calls Martin Scorsese's The Aviator "the most traditional, Oscar-baity, Old Hollywood biography" he has made — both using the same vocabulary of prediction and campaign-style positioning ahead of the ceremony.
The corpus also shows the season's residue outside the current release cycle: composer Danny Elfman is described as having earned "four Oscar nominations for Good Will Hunting, Men in Black, Big Fish, and Milk," Eyes Without a Face's score composer Maurice-Alexis Jarre is noted as someone who "would later go on to win an Academy Award for his work on Lawrence of Arabia," and Reese Witherspoon is introduced simply as "the Oscar-winner" in an unrelated parenting interview — in each case the award functions as a durable label attached to the person's name long after the ceremony itself.
A TechCrunch piece on Google's Gemini Pro model uses the prior season's results as a factual benchmark to catch AI errors, listing the actual 2023 winners it got wrong: Brendan Fraser for Best Actor, "Navalny" for Best Documentary Feature, "All Quiet on the Western Front" for Best International Film, "Women Talking" for Best Adapted Screenplay, and "Pinocchio" for Best Animated Feature Film.

## Key Characteristics

- **Contender framing** — press describes a film as "Oscar bait" or "Oscar-baity" when its subject matter, cast, or pedigree seems engineered to attract Academy attention (doc_0094, doc_0192).
- **Predictive speculation** — outlets explicitly forecast outcomes ahead of the ceremony, e.g. Poor Things being "tipped to win a few real Oscars" (doc_0094).
- **Persistent credential** — an Academy Award win or nomination becomes a standing descriptor attached to a person's name in unrelated coverage years or decades later (doc_0165, doc_0587, doc_0177).
- **Multi-category structure** — the season spans many competitive categories beyond lead acting, including Documentary Feature, International Film, Adapted Screenplay, and Animated Feature (doc_0126).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses awards-season vocabulary ("Oscar bait," "tipped to win") without stating when the season runs or how it culminates. Per Wikipedia, the film awards season "usually begins during November or December of the previous year," with the Academy Awards ceremony as its culmination, held "commonly in late February or early March following the relevant calendar year, and six weeks after the announcement of the nominees" (Wikipedia, *Academy Awards*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# David Pakman's Venture Background At CoinFund

On TechCrunch's Chain Reaction podcast, Jacquelyn interviewed David Pakman, managing partner and head of venture investments at CoinFund.

Before CoinFund, Pakman spent 14 years at the venture capital firm Venrock. He also led the Series A and B rounds at Dollar Shave Club, which was acquired by Unilever for $1 billion. And in 1991 he co-created Apple Music when he was part of Apple's system software product marketing group.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.



---


# Apple's Privacy Stance Versus Google's Default Payments

Meagan Bellshaw's privacy line of questioning attacked the premise that Apple chose Google because Google had the best product: if Apple genuinely regards Google as bad on privacy, then something other than product quality must explain why Apple gives Google a central place on its platform.

Bellshaw asked Cue whether Apple believes user privacy is important, to which he said, "Absolutely." She then showed a series of emails and slides in which Cue and Apple railed against Google's privacy policies, and Cue readily agreed with them: "We've always thought we had better privacy than Google." He said one provision of the ISA was that Google had to allow people to search without logging in, and that Apple has done things in Safari and around its platforms to make it harder for Google or anyone else to track users. Bellshaw never quite said it, but The Verge read the DOJ's implication as this: Google is a privacy menace anathema to everything Apple believes is important to its users, yet Apple gives it that central place because Google pays so handsomely. She then asked Cue to review some of Apple's financial filings and whether it is true that the ISA represents a significant portion of Apple's profits. Cue's rebuttal was that this is not how Apple looks at it, because the framing doesn't account for all the work Apple did to make its platform so appealing that an agreement like this could work as well as it does.



---


# Expedia's Testimony On Google Ad Costs And Organic Listings

On November 1, 2023, Barry Diller, chair of Expedia and IAC, testified about his concerns that the increasing number of ads in search results was having an impact on organic listings. Quoting a letter he had written to Google back in 2019, per Bloomberg: "I must say I'm on the edge of revolt now that Google's actions are so punitive, not just for Expedia but also for IAC and all the players that depend upon something of a level playing field." Google CEO Sundar Pichai fired back that Google's travel listings was one of the most popular experiences the company built.

Expedia executives also testified about the cost of ads and how increases had no impact on search results. On October 19, 2023, Expedia's former chief operating officer, Jeff Hurst, told the court that the company's ad fees increased tenfold, from $21 million in 2015 to $290 million in 2019, and yet Expedia's traffic from Google did not increase. The implication was that this was due to direct competition from Google itself; Hurst pointed out that Google began sharing its own flight and hotel data in search results in that period, according to The Seattle Times.



---


# Independent Research And Reviews Of ChatGPT's Flaws

Independent researchers and advocacy groups repeatedly found ChatGPT and GPT-4 to be flawed in ways OpenAI's own launches did not resolve — on child safety, on toxicity, and on the vision-enabled multimodal model.

An independent review from Common Sense Media, a nonprofit advocacy group, found that ChatGPT could potentially be harmful for younger users, flagging it as potentially unsafe for kids; ChatGPT got an overall three-star rating in the report, with its lowest ratings relating to transparency, privacy, trust and safety. On multimodality, OpenAI announced that GPT-4 with vision would become available alongside the upcoming launch of the GPT-4 Turbo API, but some researchers found that the model remained flawed in several significant and problematic ways.

Two toxicity findings stand out. A Microsoft-affiliated scientific paper examined the "trustworthiness" — and toxicity — of LLMs including GPT-4; because GPT-4 is more likely to follow the instructions of "jailbreaking" prompts, the co-authors claim it can be more easily prompted than other LLMs to spout toxic, biased text. Separately, a study co-authored by scientists at the Allen Institute for AI showed that assigning ChatGPT a "persona" through the ChatGPT API — for example "a bad person," "a horrible person" or "a nasty person" — increases its toxicity sixfold; the co-authors also found that having the chatbot pose as certain historical figures, gendered people and members of political parties increased its toxicity, with journalists, men and Republicans in particular causing the model to say more offensive things than it normally would. That research was conducted using the latest version, but not the model then in preview based on GPT-4.



---


# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.



---


# Platform Owners Should Treat Developers As Partners

Tim Sweeney argued that any tech company, Apple and Google included, would be much better off in the long term if it viewed developers as awesome partners and did everything it could to support and empower them rather than get in their way financially — and said the opposite behavior at Apple and Google is what has disappointed him most.

His grounds are a comparison and a diagnosis. The comparison is Microsoft: even at the peak of the antitrust trial against Microsoft, he said, Microsoft was awesome to developers — always respectful, giving developers a great deal and treating them as partners — so that even as Microsoft was crushing corporate competitors, the developer experience was excellent. The Verge appended an editor's note that Netscape might feel differently. The diagnosis is that Google and Apple both treat developers as adversaries, trying to attack developer revenue streams and prevent them from competing with the platforms' own products, and have built massive self-preferencing schemes around excluding developers and disadvantaging third parties — which Sweeney calls very shortsighted. The warrant is that a platform's own long-term position improves when its developers thrive, and Sweeney offers Epic's own conduct as the demonstration: this has been Epic's philosophy with Unreal Engine and the Epic Games Store, where Epic wants to be "a cool partner that helps other companies succeed the way we do." He suspected such a philosophy change at Apple and Google may only come with a generational change in the companies' management.

Gemini Pro failed to get basic facts right about the 2023 Oscar winners in tests reported on 7 December 2023. After her first Chiefs game, Taylor Swift kept appearing at Kansas City fixtures and made a Saturday Night Live cameo with Travis Kelce, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

# Instagram Palestine Suppression

Through October 2023, as the humanitarian crisis in Gaza grew more dire, Instagram users, creators and Palestinian digital-rights groups reported that Meta was restricting, hiding, mislabelling or removing content about Palestine — including content that does not support Hamas and content that adheres to Instagram's Community Guidelines. The reports, gathered by TechCrunch and published 19 October 2023, span account restrictions, "sensitive" and "inappropriate" flags, hidden comments, collapsed Story reach, and disproportionate flagging of Arabic-language material.

Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr provides an example that predates the current escalation. Earlier this year she posted a handful of Reels about her family's trip to the West Bank — short travel vlogs sharing snippets of Palestinian culture, from decadent meals to dancing at her niece's wedding. "I hadn't been in a decade, so it's just like, life abroad," she told TechCrunch. She received anti-Palestine comments and then could not respond to them or use her account for 24 hours, despite not posting anything about the occupation; she suspects Instagram restricted her because other users reported her Palestine travel videos. "Fast forward to now and the same shit's happening," she said.

The belief that Meta shadowbans — limits the visibility of — content about Palestine is not new. In an Instagram Story last year, supermodel and activist Bella Hadid, who is of Palestinian descent, alleged that Instagram "disabled" her from posting content on her Story "pretty much only when it is Palestine based," said she gets "immediately shadowbanned" when she posts about Palestine, and reported her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Leen Al Saadi, a Palestinian journalist based in Jordan and host of the podcast "Preserving Palestine," said she is used to "constantly being censored"; her Instagram account was restricted last year after she posted a trailer for the podcast's first episode, which discussed a documentary about Palestinian street art under occupation. "Palestinians are currently undergoing two wars," Al Saadi said. "The first is with their legal occupier. The second war is with the entire Western media landscape, and when I say the entire landscape, I mean social media."

Creators report that engagement on their posts tanked specifically after they publicly condemned Israel's response to the Hamas attack as excessively violent. Some, like Jabr, say they were restricted from posting or going live; others say Instagram flagged their content as "sensitive," limiting its reach, or flagged it as "inappropriate" and removed it even when it adhered to the Community Guidelines. A user based in Egypt, who asked to stay anonymous for fear of harassment, said her posts usually get around 300 views, but after she began posting pro-Palestine content following the Hamas attack earlier that month her Stories would get only one to two views; she found that posting a random picture first, then a pro-Palestine post, raised the views, and said the same happened to her friends. Another anonymous user based in the United Kingdom said his view count returned to normal when he posted a cat photo: "My stories went from 100s of views to zero or a handful. I've had to post intermittent non-Gaza content in order to 'release' my stories to be viewed again."

The pattern extends beyond Stories. The Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), which documents Palestinian digital-rights violations and works directly with social media companies to appeal them, told TechCrunch it has received reports of Instagram inconsistently filtering comments containing the Palestinian flag emoji, with users reporting that such comments are flagged as "potentially offensive" and hidden. The organisation has also received countless reports of Meta flagging and restricting Arabic content, including content posted by news outlets: 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater said it has documented multiple cases of journalists on Instagram reporting the same news in Arabic, Hebrew and English but only being flagged for the Arabic version. "It's literally journalistic content, but the same wording in Hebrew and English does not get restricted," Abukhater said. "As if there's better moderation for those languages, and more careless moderation for Arabic content." As the Intercept reported, Instagram and Facebook flagged images of the al-Ahli Hospital, claiming they violate Meta's Community Guidelines on nudity or sexual activity.

Enforcement also runs inconsistent in the other direction. Al Saadi tried to report a comment saying she should be "raped" and "burned alive," left in response to her comment on a CNN post about the conflict; in screenshots reviewed by TechCrunch, Instagram replied that it did not violate the platform's Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations. # Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS)

## Definition

Daily fantasy sports (DFS) is the corpus's term for the weekly, single-slate NFL lineups that outlets like Sporting News build each week for operators such as DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, distinct from a season-long fantasy league roster (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331).

## Context

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

# Instagram Palestine Suppression

Through October 2023, as the humanitarian crisis in Gaza grew more dire, Instagram users, creators and Palestinian digital-rights groups reported that Meta was restricting, hiding, mislabelling or removing content about Palestine — including content that does not support Hamas and content that adheres to Instagram's Community Guidelines. The reports, gathered by TechCrunch and published 19 October 2023, span account restrictions, "sensitive" and "inappropriate" flags, hidden comments, collapsed Story reach, and disproportionate flagging of Arabic-language material.

Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr provides an example that predates the current escalation. Earlier this year she posted a handful of Reels about her family's trip to the West Bank — short travel vlogs sharing snippets of Palestinian culture, from decadent meals to dancing at her niece's wedding. "I hadn't been in a decade, so it's just like, life abroad," she told TechCrunch. She received anti-Palestine comments and then could not respond to them or use her account for 24 hours, despite not posting anything about the occupation; she suspects Instagram restricted her because other users reported her Palestine travel videos. "Fast forward to now and the same shit's happening," she said.

The belief that Meta shadowbans — limits the visibility of — content about Palestine is not new. In an Instagram Story last year, supermodel and activist Bella Hadid, who is of Palestinian descent, alleged that Instagram "disabled" her from posting content on her Story "pretty much only when it is Palestine based," said she gets "immediately shadowbanned" when she posts about Palestine, and reported her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Leen Al Saadi, a Palestinian journalist based in Jordan and host of the podcast "Preserving Palestine," said she is used to "constantly being censored"; her Instagram account was restricted last year after she posted a trailer for the podcast's first episode, which discussed a documentary about Palestinian street art under occupation. "Palestinians are currently undergoing two wars," Al Saadi said. "The first is with their legal occupier. The second war is with the entire Western media landscape, and when I say the entire landscape, I mean social media."

Creators report that engagement on their posts tanked specifically after they publicly condemned Israel's response to the Hamas attack as excessively violent. Some, like Jabr, say they were restricted from posting or going live; others say Instagram flagged their content as "sensitive," limiting its reach, or flagged it as "inappropriate" and removed it even when it adhered to the Community Guidelines. A user based in Egypt, who asked to stay anonymous for fear of harassment, said her posts usually get around 300 views, but after she began posting pro-Palestine content following the Hamas attack earlier that month her Stories would get only one to two views; she found that posting a random picture first, then a pro-Palestine post, raised the views, and said the same happened to her friends. Another anonymous user based in the United Kingdom said his view count returned to normal when he posted a cat photo: "My stories went from 100s of views to zero or a handful. I've had to post intermittent non-Gaza content in order to 'release' my stories to be viewed again."

The pattern extends beyond Stories. The Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), which documents Palestinian digital-rights violations and works directly with social media companies to appeal them, told TechCrunch it has received reports of Instagram inconsistently filtering comments containing the Palestinian flag emoji, with users reporting that such comments are flagged as "potentially offensive" and hidden. The organisation has also received countless reports of Meta flagging and restricting Arabic content, including content posted by news outlets: 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater said it has documented multiple cases of journalists on Instagram reporting the same news in Arabic, Hebrew and English but only being flagged for the Arabic version. "It's literally journalistic content, but the same wording in Hebrew and English does not get restricted," Abukhater said. "As if there's better moderation for those languages, and more careless moderation for Arabic content." As the Intercept reported, Instagram and Facebook flagged images of the al-Ahli Hospital, claiming they violate Meta's Community Guidelines on nudity or sexual activity.

Enforcement also runs inconsistent in the other direction. Al Saadi tried to report a comment saying she should be "raped" and "burned alive," left in response to her comment on a CNN post about the conflict; in screenshots reviewed by TechCrunch, Instagram replied that it did not violate the platform's Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations. # Acquisition

## Definition

Across the corpus, "acquisition" denotes one company buying another and taking ownership and control of it — whether framed as an all-cash purchase of a target's shares (Amazon–iRobot), an outright corporate purchase (OpenAI–Global Illumination, Microsoft–Activision Blizzard King, Palo Alto Networks–Talon/Dig), or referred to interchangeably as a "merger," "buy," or "deal."

## Context

The corpus uses "acquisition" (and its synonyms "purchase," "buy," "merger," "deal") across a wide range of industries and deal sizes, from an AI startup's first tuck-in purchase to a $69 billion mega-deal, showing the term denotes a general transaction type rather than one specific event.
Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot was priced as an all-cash offer, later cut by 15% during a lengthy EU antitrust review, illustrating how the announced acquisition price can move before a deal closes.
OpenAI's purchase of Global Illumination was described as the company's "first public acquisition," showing the term applies equally to small, non-controversial tuck-ins as to headline-grabbing mega-deals.
Microsoft's $69 billion purchase of Activision Blizzard and King — the largest acquisition in video game history — took nearly two years to clear antitrust review before completing, and the corpus notes Microsoft's prior $26 billion purchase of LinkedIn as an earlier acquisition of comparable scale.
In cybersecurity, Palo Alto Networks' pursuit of Talon Cyber Security and Dig Security for roughly $1 billion combined is framed as one of several "mega deals" and smaller tuck-ins (CrowdStrike–Bionic, IBM–Polar, Cisco–Splunk) that the corpus groups together as an industry-wide acquisition trend driven by consolidation pressure.

## Key Characteristics

- **Change of ownership and control** — the acquirer gains control of the target's assets, operations, or equity; in the iRobot case the EU's concern was specifically that Amazon would gain the ability and incentive to influence competitive outcomes on its marketplace once it controlled iRobot.
- **A negotiated price that can shift** — the iRobot deal's price fell 15% from its original $1.7 billion all-cash offer as the target took on more debt during a delayed close, showing acquisition price is not fixed until the deal actually closes.
- **Regulatory review as a gating step** — both the Amazon–iRobot deal (EU statement of objections, in-depth probe) and the Microsoft–Activision Blizzard deal (nearly two years of antitrust review before an October 2023 approval) show large acquisitions routinely require competition-authority clearance before completion.
- **Ranges from tuck-ins to mega-deals** — the same term covers OpenAI's small, low-profile purchase of Global Illumination and Microsoft's $69 billion Activision Blizzard purchase, differentiated by disclosed deal size and public scrutiny rather than by transaction mechanics.
- **Driven by consolidation dynamics** — in cybersecurity, acquisitions cluster as companies buy up specialized startups (e.g., Palo Alto pursuing Talon and Dig) partly in reaction to competitors' own acquisitions, a pattern the corpus explicitly attributes to a "swing" toward large all-in-one platforms.

# FTX's Marketing And Political Influence

FTX bought mainstream recognition through sports branding and paid celebrity partnerships, while Bankman-Fried separately cultivated political access on both sides of American politics — including, according to Lewis, a contemplated $5 billion offer to keep Donald Trump out of the next presidential race. TechCrunch documented the marketing side on 2023-10-01 and the political side on 2023-10-02.

On the branding side, the company gained somewhat mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships: in 2021 it bought the naming rights for the Miami Heat's home arena, it got its name branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos, and it partnered with celebrities including Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, as well as Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal and Naomi Osaka, among others. The 2023-10-02 account puts figures on two of those friendships and lucrative marketing deals: Tom Brady was paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million, to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Even Anna Wintour, the fashion doyenne, was in contact — she reached out over a Zoom meeting to ask SBF, whose preferred get-up was wildly curly hair, t-shirts and cargo shorts, to sponsor her Met Costume Ball.

On the political side, Bankman-Fried had close ties to U.S. regulators and government officials, many of whom he donated to. Lewis said that he met with the young crypto king ahead of him seeing Mitch McConnell to discuss how he could fund political candidates who were looking to offset Trump's influence in the Republican Party — a meeting for which the suit SBF brought was tightly balled up under his arm with his dress shoes falling out of the middle of the bundle. Lewis also claimed that SBF had concocted a plan to buy off Trump, to get him not to run again for president. "Like how much would it take to get an answer?" Lewis recounted; "There was a number that was kicking around… this was $5 billion." Lewis said Sam was never sure whether that figure came directly from Trump, and TechCrunch notes it is not known whether anything was ever wired. The giving was not one-sided: SBF also looked to back candidates on the Democratic side of the aisle.

# What SEO Is, And Why People Hate It

Search engine optimization is the practice of telling the algorithm whatever it needs to hear for a site to appear as high up as possible in search results, leveraging Google's supposed objectivity to lure people in and then, usually, show them some kind of advertising — a business model. It is less straightforward than buying the advertising space labeled "Sponsored" above organic search results; it is more like the Wizard of Oz projecting his voice to magnify his authority.

The discriminating feature is that SEO borrows credibility from a system users believe is neutral. Over time SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up "sneaker" in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike ("footwear that allows you to just do it!"). Perhaps this is why nearly everyone hates SEO and the people who do it for a living: the practice seems to have successfully destroyed the illusion that the internet was ever about anything other than selling stuff.

The reputational context in 2023 is a broad unhappiness with finding information online, which for almost everyone means the quality of Google Search results. Users call the links that come back "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Some blame Google itself, asserting that an all-powerful, all-seeing, trillion-dollar corporation with a 90 percent market share for online search is corrupting our access to the truth; others blame the SEO practitioners.

The stereotype of the practitioner is a hustler: a content goblin willing to eschew rules, morals, and good taste in exchange for eyeballs and mountains of cash — a nihilist in it for the thrills, a prankster gleeful about getting away with something. "This is modern-day pirate shit, as close as you can get," explained Cade Lee, who has over a decade working in SEO. What Lee said he has noticed most at SEO conferences and networking events is a certain arrogance: "There's definitely an ego among all of them. You succeed, and now you're a genius. Now you've outdone Google." The writer's own admitted starting position was that a bunch of megalomaniacal jerks were degrading our collective sense of reality because they wanted to buy Lamborghinis and prove they could vanquish the almighty algorithm — which, technically, constitutes many algorithms, but we think of as a single force.



---


# The SEO Naming Effect On Customer Acquisition

The Verge argued that Thai Food Near Me's name really did help the restaurant — but not through the mechanism its owners intended. The initial SEO "hack" was likely technically ineffective, but it was memorable and funny, and the joke led to many, many, many articles and forum posts about the restaurant's name, which tipped the SEO scales in its favor; all of that content, including The Verge's own story, will help the restaurant's prominence on Google platforms. One SEO trick, the reporter wrote, has eaten another.

The grounds for saying the direct hack failed are a test and a concession. A Google Maps search for "Thai food near me" from the reporter's home in Brooklyn yielded plenty of options literally near her but not Jirapraphanan's business a few miles away. Robert Sampson, a co-owner who handles much of the back-end work including SEO, followed the online discussion about the utility of the name and conceded part of it: "The people who said that [the name is] not such a good idea… I think they're responding more from a national brand campaign. It is true that if you're in California, and you type 'Thai food near me,' you're going to have a little bit of a hard time finding us. But for local search, I think the name works really well." Danny Sullivan's position was that a "near me" name is not a silver bullet for gaming the search algorithm.

The warrant connecting name to durable ranking is the feedback loop that follows a first visit. As with Thai Food Near Me, the most powerful thing an SEO-driven name might be able to do is get customers in the door; from there it is up to the business to give them a good experience, whether that is a great plate of pad see ew or the perfect haircut, and then the cycle continues — happy customers leave good reviews, and good reviews help the business's Google Maps profile rank higher. Felix Silva also uploads high-quality photos and videos to his page and shares updates, another SEO move, since some experts say active profiles can improve a business's rankings.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# FTX's Spending Served Bankman-Fried's Status, Not Philanthropy

The Verge's reporter argued that at every turn the scams at FTX and Alameda led back to making Bankman-Fried more important — not to giving money away, as his stated Effective Altruism rationale claimed. The grounds are the pattern of what the money bought: Singh testified to more than a billion dollars spent on celebrity endorsements, which made FTX very famous even though the futures platform did not operate in the US; the political donations gave Bankman-Fried influence in the highest echelons of power; and Ellison testified to venture investments that gave him more dominance in the tech world.

The warrant joining the pattern to the conclusion is that spending reveals priorities better than statements do: it is easy to lie with words and harder to lie with money. Bankman-Fried went around telling people he wanted to make a lot of money in order to give it away, an idea of the Effective Altruism movement he affiliated himself with, but the amount he funneled to his Paper Bird vehicle alone was ten times the size of his philanthropic spending as outlined by the prosecution's expert Peter Easton — and all of it was vastly outweighed by his investments, the places where he could prove he was very smart by investing in the right companies early.

# Film Awards Season

## Definition

Film awards season is the recurring stretch of the film-industry calendar in which press coverage frames new releases as Oscar or Academy Award contenders — flagging some as deliberately positioned to win ("Oscar bait") and speculating on which will actually take home a prize — while a person's past Academy Award wins and nominations continue to be cited as a lasting professional credential.

## Context

In the corpus the season shows up mainly as a lens critics apply to late-2023 releases: Polygon calls Poor Things "the unlikeliest but most effective Oscar bait" and says it is "tipped to win a few real Oscars," and in a separate piece calls Martin Scorsese's The Aviator "the most traditional, Oscar-baity, Old Hollywood biography" he has made — both using the same vocabulary of prediction and campaign-style positioning ahead of the ceremony.
The corpus also shows the season's residue outside the current release cycle: composer Danny Elfman is described as having earned "four Oscar nominations for Good Will Hunting, Men in Black, Big Fish, and Milk," Eyes Without a Face's score composer Maurice-Alexis Jarre is noted as someone who "would later go on to win an Academy Award for his work on Lawrence of Arabia," and Reese Witherspoon is introduced simply as "the Oscar-winner" in an unrelated parenting interview — in each case the award functions as a durable label attached to the person's name long after the ceremony itself.
A TechCrunch piece on Google's Gemini Pro model uses the prior season's results as a factual benchmark to catch AI errors, listing the actual 2023 winners it got wrong: Brendan Fraser for Best Actor, "Navalny" for Best Documentary Feature, "All Quiet on the Western Front" for Best International Film, "Women Talking" for Best Adapted Screenplay, and "Pinocchio" for Best Animated Feature Film.

## Key Characteristics

- **Contender framing** — press describes a film as "Oscar bait" or "Oscar-baity" when its subject matter, cast, or pedigree seems engineered to attract Academy attention (doc_0094, doc_0192).
- **Predictive speculation** — outlets explicitly forecast outcomes ahead of the ceremony, e.g. Poor Things being "tipped to win a few real Oscars" (doc_0094).
- **Persistent credential** — an Academy Award win or nomination becomes a standing descriptor attached to a person's name in unrelated coverage years or decades later (doc_0165, doc_0587, doc_0177).
- **Multi-category structure** — the season spans many competitive categories beyond lead acting, including Documentary Feature, International Film, Adapted Screenplay, and Animated Feature (doc_0126).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses awards-season vocabulary ("Oscar bait," "tipped to win") without stating when the season runs or how it culminates. Per Wikipedia, the film awards season "usually begins during November or December of the previous year," with the Academy Awards ceremony as its culmination, held "commonly in late February or early March following the relevant calendar year, and six weeks after the announcement of the nominees" (Wikipedia, *Academy Awards*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Instagram Palestine Suppression

Through October 2023, as the humanitarian crisis in Gaza grew more dire, Instagram users, creators and Palestinian digital-rights groups reported that Meta was restricting, hiding, mislabelling or removing content about Palestine — including content that does not support Hamas and content that adheres to Instagram's Community Guidelines. The reports, gathered by TechCrunch and published 19 October 2023, span account restrictions, "sensitive" and "inappropriate" flags, hidden comments, collapsed Story reach, and disproportionate flagging of Arabic-language material.

Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr provides an example that predates the current escalation. Earlier this year she posted a handful of Reels about her family's trip to the West Bank — short travel vlogs sharing snippets of Palestinian culture, from decadent meals to dancing at her niece's wedding. "I hadn't been in a decade, so it's just like, life abroad," she told TechCrunch. She received anti-Palestine comments and then could not respond to them or use her account for 24 hours, despite not posting anything about the occupation; she suspects Instagram restricted her because other users reported her Palestine travel videos. "Fast forward to now and the same shit's happening," she said.

The belief that Meta shadowbans — limits the visibility of — content about Palestine is not new. In an Instagram Story last year, supermodel and activist Bella Hadid, who is of Palestinian descent, alleged that Instagram "disabled" her from posting content on her Story "pretty much only when it is Palestine based," said she gets "immediately shadowbanned" when she posts about Palestine, and reported her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Leen Al Saadi, a Palestinian journalist based in Jordan and host of the podcast "Preserving Palestine," said she is used to "constantly being censored"; her Instagram account was restricted last year after she posted a trailer for the podcast's first episode, which discussed a documentary about Palestinian street art under occupation. "Palestinians are currently undergoing two wars," Al Saadi said. "The first is with their legal occupier. The second war is with the entire Western media landscape, and when I say the entire landscape, I mean social media."

Creators report that engagement on their posts tanked specifically after they publicly condemned Israel's response to the Hamas attack as excessively violent. Some, like Jabr, say they were restricted from posting or going live; others say Instagram flagged their content as "sensitive," limiting its reach, or flagged it as "inappropriate" and removed it even when it adhered to the Community Guidelines. A user based in Egypt, who asked to stay anonymous for fear of harassment, said her posts usually get around 300 views, but after she began posting pro-Palestine content following the Hamas attack earlier that month her Stories would get only one to two views; she found that posting a random picture first, then a pro-Palestine post, raised the views, and said the same happened to her friends. Another anonymous user based in the United Kingdom said his view count returned to normal when he posted a cat photo: "My stories went from 100s of views to zero or a handful. I've had to post intermittent non-Gaza content in order to 'release' my stories to be viewed again."

The pattern extends beyond Stories. The Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), which documents Palestinian digital-rights violations and works directly with social media companies to appeal them, told TechCrunch it has received reports of Instagram inconsistently filtering comments containing the Palestinian flag emoji, with users reporting that such comments are flagged as "potentially offensive" and hidden. The organisation has also received countless reports of Meta flagging and restricting Arabic content, including content posted by news outlets: 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater said it has documented multiple cases of journalists on Instagram reporting the same news in Arabic, Hebrew and English but only being flagged for the Arabic version. "It's literally journalistic content, but the same wording in Hebrew and English does not get restricted," Abukhater said. "As if there's better moderation for those languages, and more careless moderation for Arabic content." As the Intercept reported, Instagram and Facebook flagged images of the al-Ahli Hospital, claiming they violate Meta's Community Guidelines on nudity or sexual activity.

Enforcement also runs inconsistent in the other direction. Al Saadi tried to report a comment saying she should be "raped" and "burned alive," left in response to her comment on a CNN post about the conflict; in screenshots reviewed by TechCrunch, Instagram replied that it did not violate the platform's Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations. "The restrictions on content, especially the content that relates to Palestine, is heavily politicized," Abukhater said. "It feeds into the bias against Palestinian narrative genuinely. It really takes the balance against Palestinians in a situation where there's a huge asymmetry of power." Similar claims circulated publicly, including an October 15, 2023 post alleging that the singer Kehlani was shadowbanned after becoming vocal and changing her profile picture to "i stand with Palestine," just as Bella Hadid had been.
