# SEO Conference Culture And Its Excesses

After years of being friends online, the SEOs were eager to let loose in person, giving off what Forrester described as "that vibe of a lot of young people with access to a lot of money. And it was like, no expenses spared in New York City."

For Forrester it was the start of a long career of keynote presentations and consummate schmoozing — Clay, the father of SEO, described him as "a cruise director" on the SS SEO. The circuit has treated him well: he has attended events in Napa, Hawaii, and Barbados among many others, as well as "an infinite number of private dinners and these types of things in every city you can think of, at the most lavish restaurants," he said. "I've lost track of how many Michelin-starred meals I've had, 'cause it's now in the dozens, from my time in this industry. And I'm not going to say no to the dinner that everyone's going to, that one company is sponsoring because it's a thank you to everybody who contributed to, whatever it was, you know? And you go and everybody has a good time. You talk about the industry, and that's it. And it becomes the stuff of legends."

Over the years he has seen it all, remembering "walking into hotel rooms and it's two o'clock in the morning, there's drugs and alcohol and everything everywhere, and there's a party going on." He marveled at the audacity of his fellow SEOs: "Somebody showed up and brought her Aston Martin to a conference and parked it at the front door. Immediately got a parking ticket." When he suggested she relocate the car before it got towed, she said she would just move it to the next parking spot and get another ticket — "It's cheaper for me to leave the car parked out front and use it as a way to start conversations with potential clients than it is for me to rent a suite at the hotel and get people to go to the suite to have the same conversation." Then she offered him a joyride around Seattle, and obviously he said yes.

Representing a search engine changed the rules. Once he represented Bing, Forrester more or less stopped drinking at conferences, as had long been the case for his counterpart at Google, an engineer named Matt Cutts, who helped build and then ran the company's web spam team before stepping back in 2014 and leaving in 2016.

# Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership

Caroline Ellison testified that she and Bankman-Fried started sleeping together in the fall of 2018, on and off, when she was a trader and he was CEO, and that they later dated twice — first from the summer of 2020 through the summer of 2021, a relationship they agreed to keep secret though some people found out, and again from the fall of 2021 until the spring of 2022, when they lived together. She was named co-CEO of Alameda with Sam Trabucco in 2021 while she and Bankman-Fried were broken up, and CEO in 2022; the goal, Bankman-Fried told her, was to "optically" separate Alameda Research and FTX. "The whole time we were dating, he was my boss at work," she said. They broke up because she wanted more from the relationship and he was distant and not paying enough attention to her. He did not grant her equity even though she asked, telling her it would be too complicated; instead she got a $200,000 salary, even as CEO, and bonuses twice a year ranging from $100,000 to $20 million.

Bankman-Fried gave a different rationale for the handover. In 2021, he testified, FTX was growing to millions of users with $1 billion of revenue, he was working 12 to 22 hours a day and taking one day off every couple of months, and because FTX had grown so much he could no longer run both companies — so he handed Alameda off to Ellison and Trabucco, who immediately after being named co-CEO promptly drifted away to early retirement. Bankman-Fried did remain involved in hedging and risk at Alameda.

Ellison's proximity also gave her an unusual view of his character. She said Alameda was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018: "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized." Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived; when she asked Bankman-Fried why he had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in the job offer, "He hadn't known how to tell me," she said. She described him as "very ambitious," said he told her there was a 5 percent chance he would become president of the United States, and said he told her that if there were a coin flip where tails destroyed the world and heads made the world twice as good, he would flip the coin — which he called being "risk-neutral," and which The Verge's reporter called a fancy way of saying he was a gambling addict. He made her CEO of his sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give her equity.

# DeepMind's Ethics Board And Its Single Meeting In 2015

When Musk invested in DeepMind he broke his own informal rule that he would not invest in any company he didn't run himself, and the downsides were already apparent when, only a month or so after his birthday spat with Larry Page, he again found himself face to face with his former friend. The occasion was the first meeting of DeepMind's ethics board on 14 August 2015, a board set up at the insistence of the startup's founders to ensure their technology did no harm after the sale. The members convened in a conference room just outside Musk's office at SpaceX, but that is where Musk's control ended: when Google bought DeepMind it bought the whole thing, and Musk was out, financially ahead but unhappy. Three Google executives now firmly in control of DeepMind were there, Page, Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder and Tesla investor, and Eric Schmidt, Google's chair, along with other attendees including Reid Hoffman, another PayPal founder, and Toby Ord, an Australian philosopher studying "existential risk".

The DeepMind founders reported that they were pushing ahead with their work but were aware the technology carried serious risks. Mustafa Suleyman gave a presentation called "The Pitchforkers Are Coming", telling the board that AI could lead to an explosion in disinformation and fretting that as the technology replaced countless jobs in coming years the public would accuse Google of stealing their livelihoods, so Google would need to share its wealth with the millions who could no longer find work and provide a "universal basic income". Musk agreed, but it was pretty clear the Google guests were not prepared to embark on a redistribution of their wealth: Schmidt said he thought the worries were completely overblown, and Page, in his usual whisper, agreed, arguing AI would create more jobs than it took away. Eight months later DeepMind had a breakthrough that stunned the AI community and the world, when a DeepMind machine called AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the ancient game of Go, a match streamed over the internet and watched by 200 million people across the globe, though most researchers had assumed AI needed another 10 years to muster the ingenuity to do that; the South Korean professional Lee Se-dol played Go against AlphaGo in March 2016.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. # Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

# iPhone Setup And The Absence Of A Search Engine Choice Screen

Eddy Cue acknowledged on the stand that the ISA didn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup — and said he wouldn't want to do that anyway, because "we try to get people up and running as fast as possible" and "setup is just critical stuff."

Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw built to that answer through a series of questions about the iPhone setup process, using three screenshots: the Appearance screen that appears when you first boot up an iPhone so you can pick font sizes, the location-tracking prompt that appears when you open Maps, and the App Tracking Transparency pop-up that tells you when an app wants to collect your data. Cue objected to all of these being considered part of setup, but Bellshaw's point was that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, and that search could be one of them. Cue argued that showing people a bunch of search engines they had never heard of would just be a bad user experience — even he couldn't remember the names of some of the alternatives to Google — and said, "We make Google be the default search engine because we've always thought it was the best. We pick the best one and let users easily change it." The Verge noted that "easily" is a persistent point of contention in the trial: DuckDuckGo's CEO, who testified the week before, claimed it takes "too many steps" to switch.

# ChatGPT Web Browsing And Plugins

OpenAI formally launched an internet-browsing feature for ChatGPT, ending the chatbot's confinement to training data up to September 2021 — a launch that came some three weeks after the feature was re-introduced in beta following several months in hiatus.

The path there ran through plugins and a withdrawal. OpenAI first connected ChatGPT to the internet by launching plugins, extending the bot's functionality by granting it access to third-party knowledge sources and databases, including the web; plugins were available in alpha to ChatGPT users and developers on the waitlist, with OpenAI saying it would initially prioritize a small number of developers and premium ChatGPT Plus subscribers before rolling out larger-scale and API access. OpenAI then announced that ChatGPT Plus subscribers could use a feature in the app called Browsing, which allows ChatGPT to search Bing for answers; it is enabled from the New Features section of app settings by selecting "GPT-4" in the model switcher and choosing "Browse with Bing" from the drop-down list, and it is available on both the iOS and Android apps. That web browsing capability for Plus subscribers, offered in July, was taken away after users exploited it to get around paywalls.

OpenAI posted on Twitter/X on September 27, 2023 that "ChatGPT can now browse the internet to provide you with current and authoritative information, complete with direct links to sources. It is no longer limited to data before September 2021."

# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.

# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."

# Film Awards Season

## Definition

Film awards season is the recurring stretch of the film-industry calendar in which press coverage frames new releases as Oscar or Academy Award contenders — flagging some as deliberately positioned to win ("Oscar bait") and speculating on which will actually take home a prize — while a person's past Academy Award wins and nominations continue to be cited as a lasting professional credential.

## Context

In the corpus the season shows up mainly as a lens critics apply to late-2023 releases: Polygon calls Poor Things "the unlikeliest but most effective Oscar bait" and says it is "tipped to win a few real Oscars," and in a separate piece calls Martin Scorsese's The Aviator "the most traditional, Oscar-baity, Old Hollywood biography" he has made — both using the same vocabulary of prediction and campaign-style positioning ahead of the ceremony.
The corpus also shows the season's residue outside the current release cycle: composer Danny Elfman is described as having earned "four Oscar nominations for Good Will Hunting, Men in Black, Big Fish, and Milk," Eyes Without a Face's score composer Maurice-Alexis Jarre is noted as someone who "would later go on to win an Academy Award for his work on Lawrence of Arabia," and Reese Witherspoon is introduced simply as "the Oscar-winner" in an unrelated parenting interview — in each case the award functions as a durable label attached to the person's name long after the ceremony itself.
A TechCrunch piece on Google's Gemini Pro model uses the prior season's results as a factual benchmark to catch AI errors, listing the actual 2023 winners it got wrong: Brendan Fraser for Best Actor, "Navalny" for Best Documentary Feature, "All Quiet on the Western Front" for Best International Film, "Women Talking" for Best Adapted Screenplay, and "Pinocchio" for Best Animated Feature Film.

## Key Characteristics

- **Contender framing** — press describes a film as "Oscar bait" or "Oscar-baity" when its subject matter, cast, or pedigree seems engineered to attract Academy attention (doc_0094, doc_0192).
- **Predictive speculation** — outlets explicitly forecast outcomes ahead of the ceremony, e.g. Poor Things being "tipped to win a few real Oscars" (doc_0094).
- **Persistent credential** — an Academy Award win or nomination becomes a standing descriptor attached to a person's name in unrelated coverage years or decades later (doc_0165, doc_0587, doc_0177).
- **Multi-category structure** — the season spans many competitive categories beyond lead acting, including Documentary Feature, International Film, Adapted Screenplay, and Animated Feature (doc_0126).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses awards-season vocabulary ("Oscar bait," "tipped to win") without stating when the season runs or how it culminates. Per Wikipedia, the film awards season "usually begins during November or December of the previous year," with the Academy Awards ceremony as its culmination, held "commonly in late February or early March following the relevant calendar year, and six weeks after the announcement of the nominees" (Wikipedia, *Academy Awards*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.

On November 21, 2023, OpenAI announced that it and Sam Altman had "reached an agreement in principle" for him to return as the company's CEO, alongside a restructured "initial" board of directors.

The new initial board named in the announcement comprised former Salesforce chief executive Bret Taylor as chair, former US Secretary of the Treasury Larry Summers, and Quora founder Adam D'Angelo. # Adam Yedidia's First Testimony And His Immunity Deal

Late in the afternoon of the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the government called Adam Yedidia to the stand, and lead prosecutor Danielle Sassoon disclosed that this college friend of Bankman-Fried had legal immunity during his testimony. Asked why he had made such a deal with the government, Yedidia answered: "I was concerned that I had unwittingly written code that contributed to a crime."

Yedidia, described as a fast-talking graduate of MIT, testified that he and Bankman-Fried were close friends in college. After Bankman-Fried left Jane Street — the high-frequency trading firm where the former billionaire got his start in finance after MIT — he persuaded Yedidia to join him, first as a trader at Alameda and then as a developer at FTX.

The testimony was cut short when the clock neared 4:30 p.m. and court adjourned for the day. # Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# SEO Conference Culture And Its Excesses

After years of being friends online, the SEOs were eager to let loose in person, giving off what Forrester described as "that vibe of a lot of young people with access to a lot of money. And it was like, no expenses spared in New York City."

For Forrester it was the start of a long career of keynote presentations and consummate schmoozing — Clay, the father of SEO, described him as "a cruise director" on the SS SEO. The circuit has treated him well: he has attended events in Napa, Hawaii, and Barbados among many others, as well as "an infinite number of private dinners and these types of things in every city you can think of, at the most lavish restaurants," he said. "I've lost track of how many Michelin-starred meals I've had, 'cause it's now in the dozens, from my time in this industry. And I'm not going to say no to the dinner that everyone's going to, that one company is sponsoring because it's a thank you to everybody who contributed to, whatever it was, you know? And you go and everybody has a good time. You talk about the industry, and that's it. And it becomes the stuff of legends."

Over the years he has seen it all, remembering "walking into hotel rooms and it's two o'clock in the morning, there's drugs and alcohol and everything everywhere, and there's a party going on." He marveled at the audacity of his fellow SEOs: "Somebody showed up and brought her Aston Martin to a conference and parked it at the front door. Immediately got a parking ticket." When he suggested she relocate the car before it got towed, she said she would just move it to the next parking spot and get another ticket — "It's cheaper for me to leave the car parked out front and use it as a way to start conversations with potential clients than it is for me to rent a suite at the hotel and get people to go to the suite to have the same conversation." Then she offered him a joyride around Seattle, and obviously he said yes.

Representing a search engine changed the rules. # Thai Food Near Me's Customer Experience

For a group The Verge's reporter spoke with at Thai Food Near Me on an evening in August, the SEO plan had — at least practically — the intended effect. One of the diners, Travis, found the restaurant on Yelp when searching for nearby dining options after missing an earlier reservation elsewhere; several people in the group had heard about the restaurant when it went viral in the spring but had not realized it was in New York. The group agreed the food was good, even though they had not known what to expect, and said they would definitely consider coming back if they were in the area.

"After you get that initial bunch, you've got people who enjoyed their dining experience here," he says. "They'll tell all their friends and family if they liked it, and then those people come from word of mouth."

Jirapraphanan wants people to come back because they actually like the food — the name is part, but not all, of the branding. "I want to be different from other Thai restaurants," he says. # Cloud Computing

## Definition

Cloud computing, in the corpus, is the named vendor-run industry that Microsoft's OpenAI deal plugged into — when the deal closed in 2019, Microsoft "had a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service" — and that later commentary treats as the historical template for AI-market dynamics like vendor lock-in, market consolidation, and billing norms.

## Context

In the corpus, cloud computing shows up mainly as the historical precedent and infrastructural backbone for the current AI boom, rather than as a subject in its own right.

Commentators reach for the cloud computing industry to explain both OpenAI's near-collapse and the shape of the AI market that followed it: the industry became renowned for locking companies into "centralized, vortex-like silos," which is offered as the reason so many startups panicked and contacted OpenAI's rivals when OpenAI itself looked like it might disintegrate.

The same precedent is used to forecast how the AI market layers will settle: the foundation-model layer is expected to "settle into an oligopolistic structure like the cloud provider market," and, separately, incumbents in cloud computing (like those in the earlier internet buildout) are said to have kept innovating "until innovation becomes stagnant" — a pattern predicted to repeat for AI incumbents.

Cloud computing also appears as a budget line competing with AI spending — total AI spending has overtaken cloud computing spending even though cloud computing "remains critical" — and as a unit-economics contrast: AI compute is normally metered in raw processing terms (FLOPs) or dollars per day, a different and less mature billing metric than most cloud computing's established consumption pricing.

## Key Characteristics

- **Centralized, provider-hosted delivery** — cloud computing is a vendor's service that a customer builds on top of, illustrated by Microsoft's use of its "cloud computing service" as the integration point for OpenAI's models.
- **Lock-in and the multi-cloud response** — the cloud computing industry is described as having locked customers into single-vendor "silos," which pushed companies toward multi-cloud and hybrid strategies — a dynamic the corpus draws on directly to explain AI startups' current over-reliance on OpenAI.
- **Tendency toward an oligopolistic market structure** — cloud computing is used as the reference case for a market that consolidated around a few large "cloud provider" incumbents, the same structure forecast for the foundation-model layer of the AI stack.
- **Incumbent-innovate-then-stagnate pattern** — cloud computing (alongside the internet) is cited as a precedent where incumbents keep innovating only until the market matures and stagnates, opening room for new entrants.
- **Compute as a metered, regulable resource** — "compute" (processing capacity, measured in floating point operations or FLOPs) is treated as a quantifiable input separate from "cloud computing" as an industry, and it is significant enough that the EU AI Act sets its high-risk regulatory threshold for general-purpose AI models directly on cumulative training compute (10^25 FLOPs).
- **Distinct billing norms from AI compute** — cloud computing has settled consumption-pricing conventions, whereas AI compute costs (e.g., OpenAI's roughly $700,000/day compute spend) are tracked and priced differently, "a very different metric than most cloud computing."

## Background (external)

More broadly (outside this corpus), cloud computing is a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources — such as networks, servers, storage, applications, and services — that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort (NIST, "NIST Definition of Cloud Computing", accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.nist.gov/publications/nist-definition-cloud-computing).

# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. OpenAI faced regulatory action on several fronts in 2023: Italy ordered ChatGPT blocked over GDPR concerns, Poland opened its own GDPR investigation, China's licensing regime pushed ChatGPT clients out of the App Store, and the FTC was reported to be investigating the chatbot's statements about people.

# Content Moderation

## Definition

Content moderation, as the corpus uses the term, is the mix of platform policy and enforcement — written rules like Meta's Violence and Incitement policy and Community Guidelines, human reviewers, automated systems, and crowdsourced tools like X's Community Notes — that decides what user-generated content stays visible and how a platform acts on notices of illegal or rule-breaking material.

## Context

In the corpus, content moderation surfaces mainly as the practice EU regulators scrutinize under the Digital Services Act (DSA): the DSA's "very precise obligations" require platforms to be "timely, diligent and objective" in acting on notices of illegal content, and the European Commission's formal DSA proceeding against X names "content moderation" as one of the specific areas under investigation, alongside risk management, dark patterns, advertising transparency, and researcher data access (doc_0024; doc_0153).
It also appears as a site of contested practice and bias: Meta's moderation of Palestinian-related content during the Israel-Hamas war produced widespread allegations of shadowbanning and inconsistent enforcement across Arabic versus Hebrew content (doc_0106), while Meta separately described tightening its livestreaming and hostage-content moderation in direct response to that same conflict (doc_0335).
The term also frames platform-differentiation debates outside the EU: Kick's "light moderation" is cited as both a draw for streamers leaving Twitch and a source of safety controversy (doc_0405), Mozilla frames robust moderation and "trust and safety" as central to its fediverse strategy while noting a stricter-moderation rival (Pebble) failed to grow (doc_0026), and the US Supreme Court case over Texas and Florida laws turns on whether content moderation is a form of constitutionally protected "editorial judgment" (doc_0256).

## Key Characteristics

- **Policy plus enforcement** — moderation combines written rules (e.g. Meta's Violence and Incitement policy, Community Guidelines) with mechanisms to act on them: human reviewers, automated classifiers, and appeals processes (doc_0335; doc_0106).
- **Legally obligated for large platforms under the DSA** — the DSA requires timely, diligent, objective action on illegal-content notices, and imposes added systemic-risk mitigation duties (e.g. disinformation) on very large online platforms like X and Meta (doc_0024; doc_0335).
- **Can be outsourced/crowdsourced** — X replaced parts of its formal moderation function with the crowdsourced "Community Notes" system after gutting in-house enforcement teams, a shift EU regulators are explicitly assessing for adequacy (doc_0025; doc_0153).
- **Prone to inconsistency and bias** — Meta's own third-party report found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content, and attributed this to uneven language/dialect resources and reviewer training rather than deliberate policy (doc_0106).
- **Contested as speech regulation** — in the US, whether moderation decisions constitute protected "editorial judgment" under the First Amendment is the central legal question in the Texas/Florida social-media laws before the Supreme Court (doc_0256).
- **A competitive and reputational lever** — platforms position their moderation stance (heavy vs. light) as a market differentiator (doc_0508; doc_0405), though the corpus notes stricter moderation alone did not guarantee growth for at least one platform, Pebble, which shut down after never gaining more than 20,000 users (doc_0026).

## Background (external)

The corpus repeatedly uses "content moderation" without ever stating a general definition for it. Content moderation, more broadly, is the systematic practice of screening user-generated content and applying a predetermined set of rules to determine whether it should be published, removed, or restricted — commonly for material judged irrelevant, obscene, illegal, harmful, or insulting — either by removing it outright, labeling it, or letting users filter it themselves (Wikipedia, *Content moderation*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.

# Instagram Palestine Suppression

Through October 2023, as the humanitarian crisis in Gaza grew more dire, Instagram users, creators and Palestinian digital-rights groups reported that Meta was restricting, hiding, mislabelling or removing content about Palestine — including content that does not support Hamas and content that adheres to Instagram's Community Guidelines. The reports, gathered by TechCrunch and published 19 October 2023, span account restrictions, "sensitive" and "inappropriate" flags, hidden comments, collapsed Story reach, and disproportionate flagging of Arabic-language material.

Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr provides an example that predates the current escalation. Earlier this year she posted a handful of Reels about her family's trip to the West Bank — short travel vlogs sharing snippets of Palestinian culture, from decadent meals to dancing at her niece's wedding. "I hadn't been in a decade, so it's just like, life abroad," she told TechCrunch. She received anti-Palestine comments and then could not respond to them or use her account for 24 hours, despite not posting anything about the occupation; she suspects Instagram restricted her because other users reported her Palestine travel videos. "Fast forward to now and the same shit's happening," she said.

The belief that Meta shadowbans — limits the visibility of — content about Palestine is not new. In an Instagram Story last year, supermodel and activist Bella Hadid, who is of Palestinian descent, alleged that Instagram "disabled" her from posting content on her Story "pretty much only when it is Palestine based," said she gets "immediately shadowbanned" when she posts about Palestine, and reported her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Leen Al Saadi, a Palestinian journalist based in Jordan and host of the podcast "Preserving Palestine," said she is used to "constantly being censored"; her Instagram account was restricted last year after she posted a trailer for the podcast's first episode, which discussed a documentary about Palestinian street art under occupation. "Palestinians are currently undergoing two wars," Al Saadi said. "The first is with their legal occupier. The second war is with the entire Western media landscape, and when I say the entire landscape, I mean social media."

Creators report that engagement on their posts tanked specifically after they publicly condemned Israel's response to the Hamas attack as excessively violent. Some, like Jabr, say they were restricted from posting or going live; others say Instagram flagged their content as "sensitive," limiting its reach, or flagged it as "inappropriate" and removed it even when it adhered to the Community Guidelines. A user based in Egypt, who asked to stay anonymous for fear of harassment, said her posts usually get around 300 views, but after she began posting pro-Palestine content following the Hamas attack earlier that month her Stories would get only one to two views; she found that posting a random picture first, then a pro-Palestine post, raised the views, and said the same happened to her friends. Another anonymous user based in the United Kingdom said his view count returned to normal when he posted a cat photo: "My stories went from 100s of views to zero or a handful. I've had to post intermittent non-Gaza content in order to 'release' my stories to be viewed again."

The pattern extends beyond Stories. The Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), which documents Palestinian digital-rights violations and works directly with social media companies to appeal them, told TechCrunch it has received reports of Instagram inconsistently filtering comments containing the Palestinian flag emoji, with users reporting that such comments are flagged as "potentially offensive" and hidden. The organisation has also received countless reports of Meta flagging and restricting Arabic content, including content posted by news outlets: 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater said it has documented multiple cases of journalists on Instagram reporting the same news in Arabic, Hebrew and English but only being flagged for the Arabic version. "It's literally journalistic content, but the same wording in Hebrew and English does not get restricted," Abukhater said. "As if there's better moderation for those languages, and more careless moderation for Arabic content." As the Intercept reported, Instagram and Facebook flagged images of the al-Ahli Hospital, claiming they violate Meta's Community Guidelines on nudity or sexual activity.

Enforcement also runs inconsistent in the other direction. Al Saadi tried to report a comment saying she should be "raped" and "burned alive," left in response to her comment on a CNN post about the conflict; in screenshots reviewed by TechCrunch, Instagram replied that it did not violate the platform's Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations. "The restrictions on content, especially the content that relates to Palestine, is heavily politicized," Abukhater said. "It feeds into the bias against Palestinian narrative genuinely. It really takes the balance against Palestinians in a situation where there's a huge asymmetry of power." Similar claims circulated publicly, including an October 15, 2023 post alleging that the singer Kehlani was shadowbanned after becoming vocal and changing her profile picture to "i stand with Palestine," just as Bella Hadid had been.

# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Film Awards Season

## Definition

Film awards season is the recurring stretch of the film-industry calendar in which press coverage frames new releases as Oscar or Academy Award contenders — flagging some as deliberately positioned to win ("Oscar bait") and speculating on which will actually take home a prize — while a person's past Academy Award wins and nominations continue to be cited as a lasting professional credential.

## Context

In the corpus the season shows up mainly as a lens critics apply to late-2023 releases: Polygon calls Poor Things "the unlikeliest but most effective Oscar bait" and says it is "tipped to win a few real Oscars," and in a separate piece calls Martin Scorsese's The Aviator "the most traditional, Oscar-baity, Old Hollywood biography" he has made — both using the same vocabulary of prediction and campaign-style positioning ahead of the ceremony.
The corpus also shows the season's residue outside the current release cycle: composer Danny Elfman is described as having earned "four Oscar nominations for Good Will Hunting, Men in Black, Big Fish, and Milk," Eyes Without a Face's score composer Maurice-Alexis Jarre is noted as someone who "would later go on to win an Academy Award for his work on Lawrence of Arabia," and Reese Witherspoon is introduced simply as "the Oscar-winner" in an unrelated parenting interview — in each case the award functions as a durable label attached to the person's name long after the ceremony itself.
A TechCrunch piece on Google's Gemini Pro model uses the prior season's results as a factual benchmark to catch AI errors, listing the actual 2023 winners it got wrong: Brendan Fraser for Best Actor, "Navalny" for Best Documentary Feature, "All Quiet on the Western Front" for Best International Film, "Women Talking" for Best Adapted Screenplay, and "Pinocchio" for Best Animated Feature Film.

- **Predictive speculation** — outlets explicitly forecast outcomes ahead of the ceremony, e.g. Poor Things being "tipped to win a few real Oscars" (doc_0094).

# Instagram Palestine Suppression

Through October 2023, as the humanitarian crisis in Gaza grew more dire, Instagram users, creators and Palestinian digital-rights groups reported that Meta was restricting, hiding, mislabelling or removing content about Palestine — including content that does not support Hamas and content that adheres to Instagram's Community Guidelines. The reports, gathered by TechCrunch and published 19 October 2023, span account restrictions, "sensitive" and "inappropriate" flags, hidden comments, collapsed Story reach, and disproportionate flagging of Arabic-language material.

Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr provides an example that predates the current escalation. Earlier this year she posted a handful of Reels about her family's trip to the West Bank — short travel vlogs sharing snippets of Palestinian culture, from decadent meals to dancing at her niece's wedding. "I hadn't been in a decade, so it's just like, life abroad," she told TechCrunch. She received anti-Palestine comments and then could not respond to them or use her account for 24 hours, despite not posting anything about the occupation; she suspects Instagram restricted her because other users reported her Palestine travel videos. "Fast forward to now and the same shit's happening," she said.

The belief that Meta shadowbans — limits the visibility of — content about Palestine is not new. In an Instagram Story last year, supermodel and activist Bella Hadid, who is of Palestinian descent, alleged that Instagram "disabled" her from posting content on her Story "pretty much only when it is Palestine based," said she gets "immediately shadowbanned" when she posts about Palestine, and reported her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Leen Al Saadi, a Palestinian journalist based in Jordan and host of the podcast "Preserving Palestine," said she is used to "constantly being censored"; her Instagram account was restricted last year after she posted a trailer for the podcast's first episode, which discussed a documentary about Palestinian street art under occupation. "Palestinians are currently undergoing two wars," Al Saadi said. "The first is with their legal occupier. The second war is with the entire Western media landscape, and when I say the entire landscape, I mean social media."

Creators report that engagement on their posts tanked specifically after they publicly condemned Israel's response to the Hamas attack as excessively violent. Some, like Jabr, say they were restricted from posting or going live; others say Instagram flagged their content as "sensitive," limiting its reach, or flagged it as "inappropriate" and removed it even when it adhered to the Community Guidelines. A user based in Egypt, who asked to stay anonymous for fear of harassment, said her posts usually get around 300 views, but after she began posting pro-Palestine content following the Hamas attack earlier that month her Stories would get only one to two views; she found that posting a random picture first, then a pro-Palestine post, raised the views, and said the same happened to her friends. Another anonymous user based in the United Kingdom said his view count returned to normal when he posted a cat photo: "My stories went from 100s of views to zero or a handful. I've had to post intermittent non-Gaza content in order to 'release' my stories to be viewed again."

The pattern extends beyond Stories. The Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), which documents Palestinian digital-rights violations and works directly with social media companies to appeal them, told TechCrunch it has received reports of Instagram inconsistently filtering comments containing the Palestinian flag emoji, with users reporting that such comments are flagged as "potentially offensive" and hidden. The organisation has also received countless reports of Meta flagging and restricting Arabic content, including content posted by news outlets: 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater said it has documented multiple cases of journalists on Instagram reporting the same news in Arabic, Hebrew and English but only being flagged for the Arabic version. "It's literally journalistic content, but the same wording in Hebrew and English does not get restricted," Abukhater said. "As if there's better moderation for those languages, and more careless moderation for Arabic content." As the Intercept reported, Instagram and Facebook flagged images of the al-Ahli Hospital, claiming they violate Meta's Community Guidelines on nudity or sexual activity.

Enforcement also runs inconsistent in the other direction. Al Saadi tried to report a comment saying she should be "raped" and "burned alive," left in response to her comment on a CNN post about the conflict; in screenshots reviewed by TechCrunch, Instagram replied that it did not violate the platform's Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations. # The Timing Trade-Off In Rookie Of The Year Futures Betting

There is a fixed trade-off in when to bet NBA Rookie of the Year futures: the earlier you bet, the better the odds, but you bet without much information that could be key to an educated decision; conversely, if you wait for the data you need for an informed bet, the odds tighten and you see less of a return.

The mechanism is symmetric between bettor and book. When the lines are first released, the season has not started, so there are no statistics, trends or player news — the pre-season odds are so favorable precisely because even the oddsmakers lack the data to craft more specific lines. Once the season starts and you can see how the rookies are performing, you can gather the relevant data; but sportsbooks are gathering the same information and tighten the Rookie of the Year lines in response. So while you can better guess who will hoist the Wilt Chamberlain Trophy, the odds are tighter and your potential return reduced.

Stated as pros and cons: betting early gives an opportunity to find better value and betting odds that are fresh and unadjusted, but carries much higher risk because a player's performance, health and team dynamic can change through the season, and offers limited information. Waiting gives a lot more information for an informed bet and avoids betting on a player not remotely in contention, but reduces the opportunity to find value and the odds may not be as favorable. The range over which this holds is bounded by the individual: it is always important to take your risk tolerance into consideration while weighing the potential rewards, and no matter when you decide to wager, always gather as much information as possible before risking your money.

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

# Film Awards Season

## Definition

Film awards season is the recurring stretch of the film-industry calendar in which press coverage frames new releases as Oscar or Academy Award contenders — flagging some as deliberately positioned to win ("Oscar bait") and speculating on which will actually take home a prize — while a person's past Academy Award wins and nominations continue to be cited as a lasting professional credential.

## Context

In the corpus the season shows up mainly as a lens critics apply to late-2023 releases: Polygon calls Poor Things "the unlikeliest but most effective Oscar bait" and says it is "tipped to win a few real Oscars," and in a separate piece calls Martin Scorsese's The Aviator "the most traditional, Oscar-baity, Old Hollywood biography" he has made — both using the same vocabulary of prediction and campaign-style positioning ahead of the ceremony.
The corpus also shows the season's residue outside the current release cycle: composer Danny Elfman is described as having earned "four Oscar nominations for Good Will Hunting, Men in Black, Big Fish, and Milk," Eyes Without a Face's score composer Maurice-Alexis Jarre is noted as someone who "would later go on to win an Academy Award for his work on Lawrence of Arabia," and Reese Witherspoon is introduced simply as "the Oscar-winner" in an unrelated parenting interview — in each case the award functions as a durable label attached to the person's name long after the ceremony itself.
A TechCrunch piece on Google's Gemini Pro model uses the prior season's results as a factual benchmark to catch AI errors, listing the actual 2023 winners it got wrong: Brendan Fraser for Best Actor, "Navalny" for Best Documentary Feature, "All Quiet on the Western Front" for Best International Film, "Women Talking" for Best Adapted Screenplay, and "Pinocchio" for Best Animated Feature Film.

## Key Characteristics

- **Contender framing** — press describes a film as "Oscar bait" or "Oscar-baity" when its subject matter, cast, or pedigree seems engineered to attract Academy attention (doc_0094, doc_0192).
- **Predictive speculation** — outlets explicitly forecast outcomes ahead of the ceremony, e.g. Poor Things being "tipped to win a few real Oscars" (doc_0094).
- **Persistent credential** — an Academy Award win or nomination becomes a standing descriptor attached to a person's name in unrelated coverage years or decades later (doc_0165, doc_0587, doc_0177).
- **Multi-category structure** — the season spans many competitive categories beyond lead acting, including Documentary Feature, International Film, Adapted Screenplay, and Animated Feature (doc_0126).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses awards-season vocabulary ("Oscar bait," "tipped to win") without stating when the season runs or how it culminates. Per Wikipedia, the film awards season "usually begins during November or December of the previous year," with the Academy Awards ceremony as its culmination, held "commonly in late February or early March following the relevant calendar year, and six weeks after the announcement of the nominees" (Wikipedia, *Academy Awards*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# NBA Props And Futures: What They Cover And When To Bet Them

NBA player and team props are growing in popularity, and sportsbooks are providing more NBA props than ever, because it is much easier to focus on a single player and how he will perform than on the entire team. Player props might cover how many points a player scores or how many rebounds he pulls down, typically provided in an over/under format. Team props range from which team will score the first bucket to the total points scored in a quarter to which team will lead at halftime, with the selection often robust, especially when high-profile teams play.

Futures bets are bets on events that will happen in the future, and Rookie of the Year is only one of them: legal online sportsbooks carry a wide selection of NBA futures. They can usually be bet throughout the year, including well before the season starts and through the regular season, and the further away from the event, the more likely you are to find heavier odds in your favor.

Alongside futures, bettors can wager on many NBA markets during the regular season and postseason. Game lines — moneylines, point spreads and totals — are the most popular, but team and player props, parlays and more are also available. The NBA is the second-most popular odds market to bet on in the US, behind NFL betting odds, which means every online betting site always has a great selection of NBA odds.

# Wearable Device

## Definition

In this corpus, "wearable device" (or "wearable") is the umbrella term outlets use for a body-worn consumer or health-tech gadget — a smartwatch, fitness ring, fitness band, or medical-sensing device — interchangeably with specific products like the Apple Watch, Google Pixel Watch, Whoop 4, Ultrahuman Ring Air, and Acurable's respiratory monitors.

## Context

The corpus uses "wearable" as the umbrella term spanning consumer smartwatches (Apple Watch, Google Pixel Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch), fitness rings (Ultrahuman Ring Air), fitness bands (Whoop 4), and specialized medical-sensing gadgets (Acurable's respiratory monitors, the Willow Go wearable breast pump). Some wearables are purely consumer-facing fitness/lifestyle products sold through holiday deals coverage, while others sit at the boundary of consumer electronics and regulated medical devices — the Apple Watch's SpO2 blood-oxygen sensor and EKG feature are the clearest example, since they triggered patent litigation with medical device makers Masimo and AliveCor over the underlying sensing technology. Acurable is described explicitly as "a medical device company that makes patient-friendly wearable devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions at home," showing wearables also serving a clinical diagnostic role outside the smartwatch category.

## Key Characteristics

- **Body-worn form factor** — worn on the wrist (Apple Watch, Pixel Watch, Whoop 4, Galaxy Watch), finger (Ultrahuman Ring Air), or elsewhere on the body (Acurable's respiratory monitors, Willow Go breast pump).
- **On-board sensing** — wearables carry sensors such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, optical heart-rate sensors, and SpO2 (blood-oxygen) sensors; the Apple Watch Series 9's double-tap gesture, for instance, is detected from accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate data collected at the wrist.
- **Companion-app dependence** — many wearables (Whoop 4, Ultrahuman Ring Air) have no display of their own and instead offload data to a smartphone app for analysis and coaching.
- **Health/medical crossover** — some wearables function as, or overlap with, regulated medical devices: the Apple Watch's SpO2 and EKG features became the subject of ITC patent disputes with medical device makers Masimo and AliveCor, and Acurable markets its wearables as home-use medical devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions such as sleep apnea.
- **Rapid feature iteration** — newer models add capabilities like Sleep Profiles, abnormal heart-rate tracking, and gesture controls (double tap), often gated behind newer chips (the Apple Watch Series 9's S9 chip with four neural engines).

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the general definition is broader than any single corpus device: wearable technology comprises small electronic and mobile devices, worn on the body or built into clothing or accessories, that commonly detect and transmit information such as vital signs, sometimes with immediate biofeedback to the wearer (Wikipedia, "Wearable technology," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wearable_technology).
